title: Burden of proof for Apocrypha and unwritten traditions lies on their defenders
source_text: XXII. Ac proinde Scripturae perfectioni nihil obest, si demonstrari per eam non possit hunc aut illum librum, qui falso Canonicus praesumitur, revera Apocryphum esse. Imo, etiamsi omnino steteret de non scriptis traditionibus, ad illas rejiciendas sufficere deberet, quod idoneis argumentis eorum authoritas suaderi & probari non potest sicuti Scripturae divinae. Neque nostrum est probare illas non esse divinas, sed eis qui illas urgent atque tuentur, probandum incumbit illas divinas esse.
pass_a_gloss: And therefore nothing stands against the perfection of Scripture if by it it cannot be demonstrated that this or that book, which is falsely presumed Canonical, is in reality Apocryphal. Nay, even if the matter of unwritten traditions stood altogether, for rejecting them it ought to suffice that by suitable arguments their authority cannot be urged and proved as that of divine Scripture. Nor is it our part to prove that they are not divine, but upon those who urge and defend them falls the burden of proving that they are divine.
pass_b_english: Scripture's perfection is not hurt if it cannot demonstrate that this or that book, falsely presumed canonical, is really apocryphal.
Even if unwritten traditions were granted for the sake of argument, it should be enough for rejecting them that their authority cannot be shown by fit arguments as divine Scripture's can.
It is not our job to prove they are not divine. Those who press and defend them must prove that they are.

lemmas.gloss: the burden of proving falls upon

choices.why: Strengthens the a fortiori on traditions.
